mappings.note: Picking the fungal disease links an illness to the group of organism causing it. Not LO-2, because diseases rather than organisms are the options.
The curd-setting bacterium is a useful microorganism. Not LO-5, which fits the souring process rather than naming the organism.
AIDS traced to HIV is a disease-to-agent link. Not LO-1, since no structural comparison is made.
Selecting the bacterial disease is the same disease-to-cause relation. Not LO-12, because no precaution is chosen.
Excluding the non-preservative is applied food-preservation knowledge for the kitchen. Not LO-2, because preservatives are not organisms being classified.
The nitrogen cycle keeping atmospheric nitrogen constant is a process to be explained. Not LO-2, because the item names a cycle rather than sorting the organisms in it.
Ranking microorganisms by size to find the smallest differentiates them on a physical property. Not LO-2, which is reserved for the useful/harmful sorting.
Identifying a bacteriophage among microbes rests on its distinctive structure. Not LO-5, because no process of infection is being explained.
Choosing the correct description of a bacteriophage tests its structural and functional characteristics. Not LO-2, since it is one organism, not a classification exercise.
Fungal reproduction by spores is a biological process to be explained. Not LO-2, because reproduction here is a mechanism, not a sexual/asexual sorting task.

Asking which characteristic places algae among autotrophs is classification by a characteristic, worded almost as the outcome is. Not LO-1, because a group membership is justified rather than two organisms told apart.
Explaining mouldy bread by warmth and moisture relates an observed phenomenon to the conditions causing it. Not LO-3, because the conditions are given rather than investigated by the pupil.
Naming the microorganisms that keep atmospheric nitrogen in balance identifies useful microbes. Not LO-5, used here for the cycle itself rather than for its agents.
Dough rising because of the carbon dioxide yeast releases is a phenomenon-to-cause link. Deliberately different from the items asking which organism is used, which sit on LO-2.
Yeast in grape juice over a week is fermentation, a process to be named and explained. Not LO-3, since the outcome is known rather than investigated.
The bacterial enzyme that digests cellulose is part of explaining digestion in herbivores. Not LO-2, because an enzyme is not an organism to classify.
Listing what microorganisms do in biotechnology is the useful side of the useful/harmful classification. Not LO-12, because no specific day-to-day action is taken by the pupil.
Products made using bacteria identify them as useful microorganisms. Not LO-5, because no process is explained, only outputs listed.
Naming disease-causing microbes as pathogens labels the harmful class in the useful/harmful classification. Not LO-4, because no particular disease is traced to its cause.
Which pathogens mosquitoes carry relates diseases to their vector. Not LO-12, since no control measure is chosen.
Identifying the protozoan disease is a disease-to-agent link. Not LO-2, because the options are illnesses.
Matching diseases to their microorganisms and symptoms is causal association across three columns. Not LO-1, because nothing is distinguished structurally.
Preventing ringworm through hygiene is a health measure applied in daily life. Not LO-4, which fits the items naming the fungus behind the disease.
The symbiotic bacterium of pea plants, Rhizobium, is the standard useful microorganism. Not LO-5, because the nitrogen-fixing process itself is not asked for.
Naming the bacterium behind cholera is a disease-to-agent link. Not LO-2, since no usefulness judgement is made.
Cellulose digested by gut bacteria in herbivores is a physiological process to be explained. Not LO-2, because a food component rather than an organism is the answer.
Penicillium as the source of a great medicine is the useful-microorganism classification. Not LO-11, because the item asks which fungus, not who discovered the drug.
Recognising Spirogyra as pond silk rests on its distinctive filamentous appearance. Not LO-2, because one organism is identified rather than a group sorted.

The feature distinguishing algae from fungi is differentiation of organisms by property and structure, the outcome word for word. Not LO-2, which would apply if they were being sorted into useful and harmful.
How Entamoeba enters the body is the route of infection, a cause-and-transmission link. Not LO-12, since no precaution is chosen.
The common cold traced to a virus is a disease-to-agent link. Not LO-1, because no structural comparison is required.
Selecting the true statement about viruses tests their distinguishing properties. Not LO-4, because no disease is traced in the stem.
How microorganisms are useful to us is the useful/harmful classification stated directly. Not LO-12, because no particular application is carried out.
The bread microorganism also making alcohol identifies yeast as a useful microbe across two uses. Not LO-5, since the fermentation change is not the question.
The usual modes of spread of infectious disease relate illness to its route. Not LO-12, because the item describes rather than prescribes.

Monomers as the units of synthetic fibre is structural knowledge of human-made fibres, which LO-1 names explicitly. This item is misfiled from the synthetic fibres chapter, but the outcome still fits its content.
Ranking fibres to find the strongest compares materials by a property, exactly LO-1. Not LO-2, because the item does not sort them into natural and human-made classes.
Fabric being made of yarn and fibre is structural knowledge about materials. Not LO-2, since no classification into groups is required.
The first man-made fibre turns on the natural versus human-made distinction LO-1 names. Not LO-11, because the item asks for the fibre, not the story of its discovery.
Naming plastics that do not remould as thermosetting classifies materials by a property. Not LO-1, because a class is being labelled rather than two materials told apart.
